unit-ww504.title: Wordly Wise · Lesson 4
unit-ww504.source: Wordly Wise 3000 Book 5, Lesson 4 (PDF in Drive)

summary.text: Word List 4 from Wordly Wise 3000 Book 5: accurate, approximate, course, depart, despair, destination, deteriorate, gale, horizon, jubilation, navigate, nostalgia, revive, sever and voyage — plus the related forms the list gives (accuracy, departure, horizontal, jubilant, navigation, nostalgic). Most of these words belong to journeys and to the sea.

why.text: This list holds together better than most, because nearly all of it is about travelling: where you are going, how you get there, the weather on the way, and how you feel about it. Learning them as a group is easier than learning fifteen separate words, and you will meet almost all of them in adventure stories.

objectives.text: Give the meaning of each of the fifteen words on Word List 4
Use the related forms correctly — accuracy, departure, horizontal, jubilant, nostalgic
Choose between accurate and approximate, which are close in topic and opposite in meaning
Say each word aloud correctly, using the pronunciation guide on every card
Spell the words whose sound and spelling do not match, like nostalgia

parentNote.text: The question bank is rebuilt to match the shape of her real vocabulary test. Her Unit 2 paper had five sections worth five marks each — a reading passage with context-clue questions, synonyms and antonyms, sentence completion, parts of speech, and word association — and the old bank here was mostly "What does this word mean?", which is the one shape that paper never uses. There are now four questions in each of the five shapes. The one difference from the paper is deliberate: it hangs five questions off a single long passage, and this app serves five shuffled questions at a time, so every question has to stand on its own. Each context-clue question therefore carries its own short passage rather than sharing one long one — measured on her phone, a 90-word passage pushes the first answer off the bottom of the screen, and she would re-read it on every question in the section. The skill is the same; only the staging differs. The cards are unchanged.

nextUp.text: Five shapes, four questions each — the same five your test uses. The parts-of-speech ones are worth slowing down on: the word's usual job is not always its job in that sentence.

cards.def:
**Correct, with no mistakes.** (adjective)
• Second meaning: able to give a correct reading or measurement — an accurate clock.
• accuracy (noun): correctness, exactness.
cards.hint: Hidden inside it is "cure" — an accurate answer has had its errors cured.

cards.def:
**Not exact, but close enough to be about right.** (adjective)
• The approximate weight of the puppy was ten pounds — near enough, not measured.
• It is the opposite of accurate, and the two are often used in the same breath.
cards.hint: It contains "proxim-", the same root as proximity, meaning nearness.

cards.def:
**The path something moves along.** (noun)
• Second meaning: a way of acting — our best course is to wait in the car.
• Third meaning: a subject you study — the science course includes field trips.
cards.hint: Three meanings, one idea: a course is the line you follow, whether through water, a decision, or a school year.

cards.def:
**To leave; to go away from a place.** (verb)
• The bus for Detroit departs at ten o'clock.
• departure (noun): the act of leaving.
cards.hint: The departures board at an airport lists everything going away.

cards.def:
**To lose hope.** (verb)
• As a noun it means a total lack of hope — the look of despair on their faces.
• Notice it is the exact opposite of optimism.
cards.hint: "De-" often means away or down. Despair is hope going away.

cards.def:
**The place someone or something is going.** (noun)
• Tell the clerk your destination when you buy your ticket.
• The destination is the end of a journey; the route is how you get there.

**To make or become worse.** (verb)
• The sidewalks deteriorated because the city did not take care of them.
• It usually happens slowly, over time, rather than all at once.
cards.hint: Things left alone tend to deteriorate. Nothing has to happen for it to happen.

cards.def:
**A very strong wind.** (noun)
• Last night's gale tore several tiles off the roof.
• Second meaning: a loud outburst — gales of laughter coming from the party.
cards.hint: A gale of wind and a gale of laughter are both something bursting out loudly.

cards.def:
**The line in the distance where the sky seems to meet the sea or land.** (noun)
• We watched the setting sun sink slowly over the horizon.
• horizontal (adjective): going straight across from side to side.
cards.hint: The horizon runs side to side, which is exactly what horizontal means.

cards.def:
**A feeling or show of great joy.** (noun)
• There was jubilation among the fans when the team won the championship.
• jubilant (adjective): very happy.
cards.hint: Bigger than pleased. Jubilation is the kind of joy that makes noise.

cards.def:
**To work out and steer the course of a ship or aircraft.** (verb)
• Sailors navigate their ships into port when they need supplies.
• navigation (noun): the science or practice of navigating.
cards.hint: "Nav-" comes from the Latin for ship. A navy sails; a navigator steers.

cards.def:
**A longing for a certain time in the past.** (noun)
• Seeing photographs of my first dog filled me with nostalgia.
• nostalgic (adjective): having that feeling.
• It is a mixed feeling — fond and a little sad at once.
cards.hint: Not quite sadness and not quite happiness. It is missing something you enjoyed.

cards.def:
**To make or become strong again.** (verb)
• A short rest will revive you.
• Second meaning: to bring back into use or fashion — the show revives old songs.
cards.hint: "Re-" means again and "-vive" means live. To revive is to bring back to life.

cards.def:
**To cut in two, or to break off completely.** (verb)
• Irving accidentally severed the garden hose while mowing the lawn.
• Also used for relationships: the two families severed all ties.
cards.hint: It looks like "seven" with the n knocked off — which is roughly what severing does.

cards.def:
**A long journey by sea or in space.** (noun)
• The voyage across the Pacific will take three weeks.
• As a verb: the Vikings voyaged across the Atlantic long before Columbus.
• A voyage is long. A quick trip across a lake is not one.
cards.hint: Sea or space only. You do not voyage to the shops.

questions.q: How is the word "deteriorated" used in this passage?
opts: To show that the boat had slowly fallen into worse and worse condition
To show that the boat had been repainted and repaired several times
To explain that the boat was built from unusually soft, light wood
To explain that the boat had been moved below deck for safe storage
questions.hint: Three details come straight after the word. What do they have in common?
steps: The word is followed by three details: eaten ropes, peeling paint, a soft plank.
Every one of them is a way the boat is worse than it used to be.
None of them is about repairs, about materials, or about where it was kept.
So "deteriorated" is telling you the boat fell into worse condition over time.

ex.main: **To show that the boat had slowly fallen into worse and worse condition.** The three details right after the word are all examples of it — that list is the clue the passage gives you.
ex.tip: When a word is followed by a list of examples, the examples ARE the definition. Read past the word before you decide what it means.

questions.passage: The lifeboat had hung on deck for thirty years, and it had deteriorated badly. Salt air had eaten through its ropes, the paint hung off in strips, and one plank was soft enough to push a thumb through.

questions.q: What do the context clues tell you a "gale" is?
opts: A thick bank of evening fog
questions.hint: The passage sets the word against another weather word on purpose.
steps: The forecast promised a breeze, which is a light wind.
"By midnight" signals that things had changed from what was promised.
Rain driven flat, and two people needed on one wheel, both mean huge force.
So a gale is a very strong wind — the opposite of the breeze promised.

ex.main: **A very strong wind.** The passage deliberately sets "breeze" against "gale", then shows you the force: rain driven flat, and two people needed on a wheel one person normally holds.
ex.tip: A contrast clue is as good as a definition. When a passage says what something was supposed to be, look for the word it is pushing against.

questions.passage: The forecast had promised a breeze. By midnight a gale was driving the rain flat across the deck, and it took two of the crew just to hold the wheel steady.

questions.q: How is the word "jubilation" used here?
opts: To describe how heavy the traffic on the road had become
To name the worry the families felt during the long wait
To name the great joy that broke out once the climbers were safe
To describe how exhausted the families were by the third day
questions.hint: Weigh all three reactions in the list, not just the strongest one.
steps: Horns, crying and laughing all come straight after the word.
They are all loud, outward reactions rather than private ones.
The moment they happen is the moment the last climber arrives safe.
So "jubilation" names the great joy that broke out at that moment.

ex.main: **To name the great joy that broke out once the climbers were safe.** Crying sits in the middle of the list, which is the trap — here it is relief, and the horns and the laughter on either side of it say so.
ex.tip: One item in a list can point the wrong way on its own. Weigh the whole list before you let a single word decide the answer for you.

questions.passage: When the last climber reached the road, the waiting families broke into jubilation. Car horns went off, someone was crying, and a woman who had not slept in two days simply sat down and laughed.

questions.q: What does this passage suggest about something on the horizon?
opts: It is hidden from view completely until the weather clears
It is close enough to be reached within an hour or so
It is directly overhead, above the mast of the ship
It is about as far off as a thing can be and still be seen
questions.hint: Ask why the trees took another three days to appear.
steps: At the horizon the island is only a gray smudge — no detail at all.
Real detail, the trees and the beach, appears only on the fourth morning.
So the horizon is the very limit of what the eye can pick out.
It is not hidden — they can see it — and it is plainly not near.

ex.main: **It is about as far off as a thing can be and still be seen.** The passage works by contrast: a smudge on day one, real detail only on day four, and three days of sailing in between.
ex.tip: "Hidden completely" is the tempting answer, but they CAN see it — a smudge is still something. Answer from what the passage reports, not from what the word sounds like.

questions.passage: For three days the island stayed a gray smudge on the horizon. Only on the fourth morning, with the sun behind them, could the crew make out trees and a thin pale line of beach.

questions.q: Which word means the SAME as accurate?
questions.hint: Think of a measurement you would trust down to the millimeter.
steps: Accurate describes something with no mistakes in it.
Careless is its opposite, so it cannot be the synonym.
Rapid is about speed and costly is about price — neither is about being right.
Exact means the same thing: correct, with nothing off.

ex.main: **Exact.** Both mean free of error. "Careless" is the word's own opposite, which is exactly why it is the option worth pausing over.
ex.tip: Check whether the question asked for SAME or OPPOSITE before you answer. The opposite is usually sitting right there among the choices.

questions.q: Which word means the OPPOSITE of depart?
questions.hint: Picture the two boards hanging in an airport.
steps: Depart means to go away from a place.
"Leave" means the very same thing, so it cannot be the opposite.
Steer is about direction and delay is about time — neither reverses it.
Arrive is the true opposite: coming in rather than going out.

ex.main: **Arrive.** Departures and arrivals are the two halves of the same board at every airport and every station.
ex.tip: "Leave" is in the list because it is a synonym. In an OPPOSITE question the synonym is the single commonest wrong answer.

questions.q: Which word means the OPPOSITE of despair?
questions.hint: Despair is what is left when one particular thing runs out.
steps: To despair is to lose hope.
Grieve and worry are unhappy feelings too, but neither is the exact reverse.
Celebrate is positive, but it is the opposite of grieving rather than of despairing.
The precise reverse of losing hope is to hope.

ex.main: **Hope.** Despair is defined by the absence of hope, which makes hope its exact opposite — closer than any other cheerful word in the list.
ex.tip: For an antonym, look for the word the target is the ABSENCE of, rather than for any word with the opposite mood.

questions.q: Which word means the SAME as sever?
questions.hint: Think what happens to a rope that is no longer one rope.
steps: To sever is to cut something in two, or to break it off completely.
Join and tie both put things together, which is the reverse direction.
Bend changes a shape without dividing anything at all.
Cut is the match: what was one piece becomes two.

ex.main: **Cut.** Severing is cutting right through, so that one thing becomes two. "Join" is the word's own opposite.
ex.tip: Two of the wrong options here put things together and one only reshapes. Sorting options by what they DO to an object makes the odd one out show.

questions.q: The ship's course...
opts: took it well south of the storm and added two days to the journey.
was delicious, especially the thick soup that arrived first.
repaired the broken mast and the torn sail before nightfall.
arrived three weeks later than the harbor master had expected.
questions.hint: A course is a path. Ask what a path can and cannot do.
steps: Here "course" means the path the ship travels along.
A path cannot repair a mast, and it cannot arrive anywhere — the ship does that.
The meal sense of "course" is real, but it does not fit "the ship's".
Only the ending about going south of the storm describes an actual path.

ex.main: **Took it well south of the storm and added two days to the journey.** That ending describes a path through the water, which is what a course is.
ex.tip: "Course" has a meal sense too, and it is among the choices on purpose. The two words before the gap — "the ship's" — are what rule it out.

questions.q: Using only a compass and the stars, the crew navigated...
opts: the sails carefully until every one of them was completely dry.
their way through three nights of open water without sighting land.
a large meal of salt beef and biscuit before turning in for the night.
and mended the hull where the collision had split it open.
questions.hint: Navigating is working out where you are and steering from there.
steps: To navigate is to work out a position and steer a course from it.
A compass and the stars are instruments for exactly that job.
Drying sails, eating and mending a hull are all other kinds of work.
Only the first ending describes finding a way across open water.

ex.main: **Their way through three nights of open water without sighting land.** Navigating is working out a position and steering by it, which is what a compass and the stars are for.
ex.tip: The opening of the sentence is the clue. A sentence-completion answer has to fit the whole sentence, not just the gap at the end of it.

questions.q: A wave of nostalgia...
opts: improved the accuracy of the charts the mapmakers had been drawing.
knocked the small boat sideways and soaked everyone sitting aboard it.
hit her the moment she smelled the pencil shavings in her old classroom.
is the name given to a strong wind that blows across tropical seas.
questions.hint: Nostalgia is a feeling, and a feeling is set off by something particular.
steps: Nostalgia is a longing for a time in the past.
A smell from a childhood classroom is exactly the sort of thing that sets it off.
A wave of feeling cannot knock a boat over or improve a chart.
So the ending about the pencil shavings is the one that fits.

ex.main: **Hit her the moment she smelled the pencil shavings in her old classroom.** Nostalgia is a longing for a time that has passed, and a smell from childhood is the classic trigger for it.
ex.tip: "A wave of" works for feelings and for water, which is why both are offered. The word straight after it decides which one you are reading.

questions.q: The hot soup and the dry blankets revived...
opts: and the storm finally passed away over the far side of the valley.
the temperature of the mountain air by a good several degrees.
the narrow route that the rescue team had marked out that morning.
the rescued hikers enough that they could walk to the road themselves.
questions.hint: Reviving brings strength back — so ask what had lost any.
steps: To revive something is to make it strong again.
Soup and blankets act on a person, not on air, a path or the weather.
The hikers are the only thing in the sentence that had lost strength.
So they are what the soup and blankets revived.

ex.main: **The rescued hikers enough that they could walk to the road themselves.** To revive is to bring strength back, and the hikers are the only thing here that had any to lose.
ex.tip: Match the ending to what the subject of the sentence could actually act on. Soup and a blanket do nothing whatever to a route or a storm.

questions.q:
The captain held a steady course all through the night.

What part of speech is "course" in this sentence?
questions.hint: Try putting "a" or "the" in front of the word and see if it still works.
steps: Ask what job the word is doing in this sentence.
It reads "a steady course" — the word has "a" in front and "steady" describing it.
Only a noun takes "a" in front and an adjective like that.
So here "course" is a noun.

ex.main: **Noun.** "A steady course" is a thing the captain held. The word "steady" describes it, and only a noun gets described that way.
ex.tip: The test for a noun: can you put "a", "an" or "the" in front of it? If you can, it is doing a noun's job in that sentence.

questions.q:
Her measurements were accurate to the nearest millimeter.

What part of speech is "accurate" in this sentence?
questions.hint: Ask which word in the sentence it is telling you about.
steps: Find the nouns first: "measurements" and "millimeter".
The word is telling you what the measurements were like.
Describing a noun is an adjective's job, not a noun's or a verb's.
So "accurate" is an adjective here.

ex.main: **Adjective.** It describes "measurements" — it tells you what kind they were.
ex.tip: An adjective answers "what kind?" about a noun nearby. Find the noun first, then check whether the word is describing it.

questions.q:
A falling rock severed the rope just above the knot.

What part of speech is "severed" in this sentence?
questions.hint: Ask what the rock actually DID.
steps: The sentence is about something that happened.
The rock is doing it, and the rope is what it was done to.
A word that takes an object like that, and changes tense, is a verb.
So "severed" is a verb here.

ex.main: **Verb.** It is the action the rock performed. The "-ed" ending and the fact that it takes an object — the rope — both mark it out as the verb.
ex.tip: A verb is the thing happening. If you can put "yesterday" at the front and the word has to change with it, it is a verb.

questions.q:
The guide gave us an approximate time for the descent.

What part of speech is "approximate" in this sentence?
questions.hint: The word is sitting between "an" and a noun. What job is that?
steps: "Approximate" really can be a verb — you can approximate a total.
But here it sits between "an" and "time".
A word in that slot is describing the noun, not performing an action.
So in THIS sentence it is an adjective.

ex.main: **Adjective.** It describes what kind of time the guide gave. The very same word is a verb in other sentences — you can approximate a distance — which is exactly why the sentence decides, not the word.
ex.tip: This is the trap that costs the most marks on a real paper: a word's usual job is not always its job today. Read the slot it is sitting in.

questions.q:
a compass, the stars, charts

Which word connects to all three?
questions.hint: What would a sailor DO with all three of these?
steps: A compass shows direction.
The stars were how sailors found their position before instruments.
Charts are maps of the water itself.
All three are tools for working out a course and steering it — navigating.

ex.main: **Navigate.** All three are instruments for working out where you are and steering towards where you mean to be.
ex.tip: Work out what the three things have in common BEFORE you read the options. Deciding first stops a plausible word pulling you off course.

questions.q:
old photographs, a song from childhood, your grandmother's kitchen

Which word connects to all three?
questions.hint: All three point in the same direction in time.
steps: A photograph, a song and a kitchen are very different things.
What they share is that each one belongs to earlier in your life.
Each is the sort of thing that brings a past time flooding back.
That longing for a time gone by is nostalgia.

ex.main: **Nostalgia.** Each one is a trigger for longing for a time that has already passed.
ex.tip: Jubilation and despair are feelings too, which is what makes them the real competition. Nostalgia is the only one pointed at the PAST.

questions.q:
rust, peeling paint, a sagging roof

Which word connects to all three?
questions.hint: All three are signs of the same process, running one way.
steps: Rust eats metal, paint peels, a roof sags under its own weight.
Every one of them takes time, and every one makes the thing worse.
Nothing here is being repaired or restored.
Getting worse over time is what it means to deteriorate.

ex.main: **Deteriorate.** All three are signs of something getting steadily worse as time passes.
ex.tip: "Revive" is the opposite and it is among the choices on purpose. Always check which DIRECTION the three things point in.

questions.q:
confetti, cheering, a medal ceremony

Which word connects to all three?
questions.hint: Ask when these three things are happening, not what they remind you of.
steps: Confetti, cheering and a medal ceremony all belong to one moment.
That moment is loud, public and happy.
Nostalgia would need the moment to be in the past and looked back on.
Great joy shown openly is jubilation.

ex.main: **Jubilation.** All three belong to a moment of great joy shown out loud and in public.
ex.tip: Nostalgia is the trap: a medal ceremony can certainly be remembered fondly years later, but the confetti and the cheering are happening NOW.
